📋AM Edition — What You Need to Know

“Futures firm as yields ease, but junk-bond stress climbs from CCC into single-B and BB”

🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.33% (intraday, 7-year +5bp). At trading day 24 (last close) it was -0.45% against a five-campaign average of -1.44% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.63%. The 10-year is +7bp since the hike vs a +20bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 762bp against a five-year average of 413bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +80bp and BB +52bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.30 → 0.61 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is moving too (+11bp in a month).
  • Bank Earnings: 8 banks reported (COF, EWBC, HWC, NIC, BKU, NTRS, ONB, OZK); 3 red-flagged (HWC: NPLs +17% QoQ; BKU: NPLs +18% QoQ; NTRS: NCO ratio +11bp QoQ). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: HWC, BKU, NTRS.
  • Stocks: Futures point higher; small caps and the Dow led yesterday's gains.
  • FX: Dollar is flat; the euro is still trading below its recent averages.
  • Technicals: S&P is well above its long-term average, but stretched versus its own history.
  • Sectors: Money is leaving tech for health care, staples and small companies.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lowest-rated junk bonds are hurting, and the stress is moving to better-rated junk.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; the weak spots are junk credit, government debt and the Gulf.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is sticky near 2.6-3%; food and energy prices are rising fast.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are high but well short of 2000; the warning signs are mixed.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Bloom Energy carries the biggest expected move; Alphabet, the largest name, reports next week.
  • Iran: Talks have stalled, Iran set tough conditions, and oil stays above $97.
  • Warsh: Fed likely holds next week; another hike remains possible by December.
  • Outlook: Short-term neutral: equities are firm but credit is quietly getting worse.
  • Trades: Own health care, cut lowest-rated junk bonds, take a tactical long in Treasuries.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 buy, 1 sell, 21 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 6.0% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads widening
  • Pre-market: Zero names cleared either rulebook, and the one "catalyst" the scanner found is a headline about IBM, not the stock it got pinned to. Empty watchlists, stale-looking data, no econ data. Today is a sit on your hands and watch day.
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.59 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 93th pctile, +21bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Stocks are calm, but the junk-bond market is flashing yellow.

Pre-market, futures are bid: ES 7778.25 (+0.30%), NQ 29851.75 (+0.59%) and Dow futures 52919 (+0.38%). That follows a broad prior session in which the S&P 500 closed 7712.57 (+0.28%), the Dow 52495.88 (+1.02%) and the Russell 2000 2773.42 (+1.65%), while the Nasdaq was flat (-0.02%). The rally is a rotation more than risk-chasing. Info Tech is down 4.81% on the week and Comm Services down 4.11%, against Health Care +5.83% and Staples +3.95%. Rates are helping: the 10Y is down to 5.0877% (-2.1bp) and Gilts are down 4.4bp to 5.366%. Europe is up, with SX5E +1.05% live. VIX is 17.14. The biggest story is below the equity surface, in high-yield credit. The Bloomberg Caa-B gap is 762bp, at the 100th percentile of its 5-year history and 234bp wider in 3 months; the Caa-B gap is the extra spread the lowest-rated junk pays over single-B. The HY dataset flags spreads as the widest since 2020-04-23. The question is whether the CCC rot is spreading, and the computed data says it is starting to. Single-B OAS is 323bp (+80bp in 1 month) and Ba is 201bp (+52bp in 1 month). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes jumped to 0.61 from 0.27 a month ago, which means junk tiers are moving together more, though it is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. IG has so far moved only modestly: 86bp, +11bp in 1 month, 37th 5y percentile. The headline index OAS (US HY 3.32%, z-score -0.63) still looks benign, which is why this matters. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Sentiment: equity complacency (VIX low, NFCI loose at -0.5) sits beside deteriorating low-grade credit, Brent at 108.51 on stalled Iran talks, and a Fed that hiked in September and is expected to pause at the Oct 27-28 meeting.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Headline spreads look calm. US IG OAS is 0.86% (z-score -0.73, 11th percentile) and US HY OAS is 3.32% (z-score -0.63, 24th percentile). EUR IG is 0.98% (z -0.62), EUR HY 3.69% (z -0.43, 41st percentile) and EM USD 1.83% (z -1.18, 8th percentile). Against crisis peaks, US HY sits at only the 12th percentile of the 2022 hike episode and 0 for GFC/COVID. EUR HY is at 15 versus COVID and 12 versus 2022. The quality breakdown is where the risk is. Bloomberg Caa OAS is 1085bp, +167bp in 1 month and +277bp in 3 months, at the 98.6th 5y percentile. The Caa-B gap of 762bp is at the 100th 5y percentile against a 5y average of ~413bp. The FRED ICE cross-check agrees: CCC 1310bp and CCC-B 974bp, both at the 100th percentile since 2023-10. The transmission is visible. Single-B is +80bp and Ba +52bp in 1 month, the B-Ba gap is +28bp in 1 month, and the HY-IG gap is 246bp, +57bp in 1 month. The Caa/B correlation rose from 0.27 to 0.61 in a month, and B/Ba from 0.79 to 0.87. IG is the firewall so far, at 86bp, +11bp in 1 month. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Key levels (analyst estimate): US HY OAS through ~3.75% would mean single-B stress is broadening into the index. That would likely need sustained equity weakness or a refinancing accident. IG above ~1.00% would mean contagion reaching high grade, most likely via a growth scare or a disorderly rates move with the 10Y above its recent 5.10% area. Holding below ~3.0% on HY would require the CCC widening to stall and the 1m change in B/Ba to reverse.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.59 vol points (15th percentile of the 48 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.7 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 93bp (steeper by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (107bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 20 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 62/100 — Core inflation is sticky but not accelerating: persistent, not re-igniting. The core-trend measures sit around their historical middle to upper middle, and most are flat to falling: Median CPI 2.61% falling, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19% falling, Core Sticky CPI 2.78% flat. Headline pressure comes from the flexible, energy-driven basket: Flexible CPI is 6.12%, rising, at its 82nd percentile. The Dallas distribution shows a two-humped basket. 28.9% of PCE components are rising above 5%, but 25.8% are falling and 27.4% sit in the 2-3% band. Core PCE at 3.01% and the 1y breakeven at 3.00% keep the Fed vigilant, while the 5y breakeven at 2.40% says longer-run expectations are anchored. Persistence is an analyst estimate.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed chart, anchored at the Oct-2022 bottom, puts the current cycle at 240.5 after 48 months. The dot-com path anchored at Oct-1990 was 235.7 at month 48 and did not peak until month 113 (1423.9). On that analogue, this rally's price path is in line with the mid-1990s, not 1999-2000. The valuation marker sits at 24% of the 2000 P/E peak. The danger this time is less retail euphoria (AAII bull-bear is -2.9pp) and more the combination of extreme index concentration (top 10 roughly 35% of the S&P 500 per Motley Fool, June 2026), a CAPE near 41 (Multpl-based, near the 44.19 Dec-1999 peak), and credit and vol complacency running past 2000 levels while CCC spreads blow out. This week's 4.81% drop in US Tech amid rotation into defensives is how froth gets deflated without a crash, if credit stays orderly. ⚔️Iran War

The conflict is unresolved and diplomacy has stalled. Per Fox News live coverage on Oct 20, Iran set red lines for any US talks: sanctions lifted, threats ended, and 'not a gram' of enriched uranium leaving the country. Per ABC News, Secretary Rubio said the nuclear question is 'at the core' of the US approach. CBS live updates report Iran's foreign minister lauding ties with Russia, contradicting President Trump's claim that Moscow gives Tehran little support. Fox's Oct 19 coverage reports Iran issuing a warning to the US as Qatar prepares to announce a regional defense agreement, with Qatari mediation continuing. CBS and NBC hub coverage also describe a contested Strait of Hormuz, with a US blockade of Iranian shipping, continued attacks on commercial vessels, and Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure. Those specifics come from aggregated coverage and were not individually verified against a dated article. Sources conflict on whether any ceasefire framework is in force. Market read (analyst): Brent at 108.51 and WTI 14.85% above its 200DMA already embed a sustained risk premium, and the near-term asymmetry is around the post-midterm (Nov 3) window.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the Oct 27-28 FOMC is the base case. In his Oct 16 Bangkok remarks, Warsh said the Fed 'removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago' and declined to prejudge meetings. Goldman Sachs economists read his and other FOMC comments as indicating an October pause (CNBC). Analyst inference: a hawkish hold, with balance-sheet language as the lever rather than the rate.

~1 YEAR

Analyst inference: one more hike is plausible by December (Goldman's base case: 'a second and final hike'). After that, Warsh's long-standing view that AI-driven productivity can be disinflationary suggests he would be open to easing through 2027 if core measures keep falling. Today's data shows Median CPI, Median PCE and Trimmed-Mean PCE all 'falling' (computed). A smaller Fed balance sheet is likely to be a durable theme, which is consistent with a steeper curve (2s10s 32.21bp computed). That last point is inferred from his prior record and not verified in this edition's searches.

Warsh is running a credibility-first Fed. Per PBS and NBC, he called price stability the key priority while refusing to signal rate moves, and he described 'a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world.' Per CNBC and Yahoo Finance, he said the economy has been more resilient than expected, credited AI investment, and warned the AI path will be 'very bumpy.' Policy implications: with Core PCE at 3.01% and the 1y breakeven at 3.00% but median and trimmed measures cooling, he has cover to pause now and keep December live. The CCC/single-B widening is the kind of financial-conditions tightening that could argue against further hikes; that is analyst inference.

Sources: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening (CNBC, Oct 16 2026) · Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but shies away from signals about rates (PBS NewsHour) · Warsh says Fed is focused on taming rising prices (NBC News) · Fed's Warsh sees AI boosting productivity but gives no signal on next rate hike (Yahoo Finance)
